claim: NICE recommends that everyone with colorectal cancer is tested for mismatch repair deficiency, either by MMR immunohistochemistry or by PCR for microsatellite instability.
needed: NICE diagnostics guidance recommends testing all people with colorectal cancer for DNA MMR-deficient tumours, by immunohistochemistry for MMR proteins or PCR for MSI.

claim: About half of all bowel cancers have this mismatch repair fault, so it's nothing unusual to find it.
needed: MSI-high is found in only about 5% of colorectal cancers (around 4% of metastatic colorectal cancer).

claim: After an operation meant to cure bowel cancer, the check-ups for the first three years include a blood marker test and CT scans of the chest, tummy and pelvis.
needed: After potentially curative surgery for non-metastatic colorectal cancer, follow-up for the first 3 years should include serum CEA and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

claim: Adjuvant chemotherapy should be given routinely to every patient with stage II colorectal cancer.
needed: The usefulness of adjuvant chemotherapy for stage II colorectal cancer has not been proven, and routine adjuvant chemotherapy for all stage II patients is not recommended.

claim: When bowel cancer has reached the lymph nodes, chemo after the operation is offered to anyone well enough for it, and it should ideally start within about six weeks.
needed: NICE guidance recommends systemic chemotherapy for all patients fit enough after surgery for Dukes' C (node-positive) colon or rectal cancer, scheduled to begin within 6 weeks of surgery.

claim: Grade 2 and grade 3 colorectal tumours have a significantly higher rate of lymph node metastasis than grade 1 tumours.
needed: The incidence of lymph node metastasis is significantly higher for grade 2/3 tumours than grade 1, and high grade is an independent predictor of nodal metastasis.

claim: Taking polyps out during a colonoscopy doesn't really change your chances of getting bowel cancer.
needed: Endoscopic polypectomy is effective in reducing colorectal cancer incidence and mortality.

claim: Even a pTis colorectal cancer needs a D3 lymph node dissection, because nodal metastasis is common at that stage.
needed: Lymph node dissection is unnecessary for pTis (M) cancer because pTis cancer is not accompanied by lymph node metastasis.

claim: Roughly one in ten pT1 colorectal cancers invading the submucosa already has lymph node metastasis, which is why a D2 dissection is done for them.
needed: D2 dissection is necessary for pT1 (SM) cancer because the incidence of lymph node metastasis is approximately 10%.

claim: If bowel cancer does come back, it's usually within the first three years after the operation, so that's when we watch most closely.
needed: More than 80% of recurrences after colorectal cancer surgery are detected within 3 years (and about 90% within 36 months).

claim: Adding CEA monitoring on top of CT surveillance gives a survival advantage over CT surveillance alone after colorectal cancer resection.
needed: The use of CEA in combination with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis does not lead to a survival advantage compared with CT alone.

claim: It's standard to have another colonoscopy about a year after bowel cancer surgery to check the rest of the bowel.
needed: Surveillance colonoscopy should be performed one year after the initial surgery for colon cancer, then generally every five years if normal.

claim: For high-risk stage II or III rectal cancer, chemoradiotherapy before surgery is the standard approach.
needed: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation is the standard of care for high-risk clinical stage II-III rectal cancer.

claim: Stage three bowel cancer means it has spread to the liver.
needed: Stage III (Dukes' C) colorectal cancer is defined by spread of the tumour to the lymph nodes.

claim: The NHS bowel screening programme sends people aged 60 to 74 a home poo test every two years, and anyone with an abnormal result is offered a colonoscopy.
needed: The NHS bowel cancer screening programme offers faecal occult blood testing every 2 years to people aged 60 to 74, with colonoscopy for abnormal results.

claim: ER, PR and HER2 status should all be assessed on every invasive breast cancer at the time of the initial histopathological diagnosis.
needed: NICE recommends assessing ER, PR and HER2 status of all invasive breast cancers simultaneously at initial histopathological diagnosis.

claim: HER2-positive cancers tend to be the slower-growing kind, so they usually do better than HER2-negative ones.
needed: HER2-overexpressing tumours grow and divide more quickly and HER2-positive breast cancer generally has a worse prognosis than HER2-negative disease.

claim: Breast cancers that have hormone receptors generally have a better outlook than ones that don't.
needed: People with hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer generally have a better prognosis than those with hormone-receptor-negative breast cancer.

claim: These aromatase inhibitor tablets work just as well whether or not you've been through the menopause.
needed: Aromatase inhibitors are only effective at suppressing oestrogen levels in postmenopausal women.

claim: Postmenopausal women with ER-positive invasive breast cancer at medium or high risk of recurrence who have taken tamoxifen for 2 to 5 years should be offered extended endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor beyond the 5-year point.
needed: NICE: offer extended endocrine therapy past 5 years with an aromatase inhibitor to postmenopausal women with ER-positive invasive breast cancer at medium or high recurrence risk who have taken tamoxifen for 2 to 5 years.

claim: Adding the HER2 drug trastuzumab to chemo after surgery cuts the chance of the cancer coming back by about half.
needed: Trials of more than 12,000 patients showed a consistent 50% reduction in recurrence risk when trastuzumab was added to adjuvant chemotherapy for HER2-positive early breast cancer.

claim: Even though it's triple negative, hormone tablets should still work well against it.
needed: Triple-negative breast cancer lacks ER, PR and HER2 receptors and is not sensitive to endocrine therapy; chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment.

claim: Triple-negative tumours account for roughly 15% of all breast cancers.
needed: Triple-negative breast cancer accounts for about 15% of all breast cancers.

claim: After breast-conserving surgery with clear margins for invasive cancer, radiotherapy to the whole breast should be offered.
needed: NICE: offer whole-breast radiotherapy to women with invasive breast cancer who have had breast-conserving surgery with clear margins.

claim: We add whole-breast radiotherapy after excision of DCIS because it improves overall survival.
needed: Adding whole-breast irradiation to surgical excision of DCIS does not improve survival, although it substantially reduces ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence.

claim: Fine-needle aspiration cytology can show malignancy, but a diagnosis of invasive carcinoma can only be made on a biopsy sample.
needed: Malignancy can be diagnosed from cytology or core biopsy, but invasive carcinoma can only be diagnosed from a biopsy sample.

claim: Because it's HER2-positive, everyone gets pertuzumab along with trastuzumab after surgery, whether or not the lymph nodes were involved.
needed: Adjuvant pertuzumab plus trastuzumab with chemotherapy is for node-positive HER2-positive early breast cancer, not node-negative disease, which is offered trastuzumab.

claim: For an early, stage one hormone-positive breast cancer, the usual course is about five years of hormone tablets, either tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor.
needed: The St. Gallen panel favours 5 years of tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitor-based therapy for stage I ER-positive cancers, extending toward 10 years for node-positive disease.

claim: HER2 overexpression is found in the majority of early invasive breast cancers, which is why anti-HER2 therapy is so widely used.
needed: HER2 overexpression is present in approximately 15% of early invasive breast cancers.

claim: Staying on tamoxifen for longer does come with a higher chance of blood clots and cancer of the womb lining.
needed: Extended use of tamoxifen carries an increased risk of thrombosis and endometrial cancer.

claim: Of everything on the report, how deep the melanoma went into the skin is the single biggest thing that tells us how it's likely to behave.
needed: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion) is the single most important prognostic factor for clinically localised primary melanoma.

claim: The Breslow number is basically how wide the spot was across the skin, so a small one is reassuring.
needed: Breslow thickness is a depth measurement, from the top of the granular layer of the epidermis (or the ulcer base) down to the deepest invasive tumour cell, not the lesion's width.

claim: For a melanoma with a Breslow thickness of up to 1 mm, the recommended lateral excision margin is 1 cm.
needed: Lateral margins are determined by Breslow thickness: 1 cm if Breslow up to 1 mm, 1-2 cm for 1-2 mm, and 2 cm above 2 mm.

claim: We'll take a really generous margin, around five centimetres, because the wider we cut the less chance it ever comes back.
needed: Wider margins give no benefit for recurrence or melanoma-related death; margins are 1-2 cm by Breslow thickness and the maximum recommended excision margin is 3 cm.

claim: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended for melanomas thicker than 1 mm.
needed: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended in melanomas over 1 mm depth (grade A, level 1a).

claim: Ulceration is just a descriptive finding on the pathology report; it isn't part of AJCC staging and doesn't independently affect outcome.
needed: Ulceration is an integral component of the AJCC/UICC staging system and an independent predictor of outcome in clinically localised primary cutaneous melanoma.

claim: Most melanomas are linked to UV from the sun or sunbeds, and people with fair skin who burn easily are at noticeably higher risk.
needed: Around 86% of UK melanomas were linked to UV from the sun and sunbeds, and fair-skinned people who burn easily are about three times more likely to develop melanoma.

claim: With melanoma it's the steady sun you get day in, day out over many years that matters, not the bad sunburns you had as a kid.
needed: Intense burning sun exposure, particularly at a young age, is a major risk factor for melanoma; chronic long-term sun exposure is instead associated with squamous and basal cell carcinomas.

claim: The ABCDE criteria, asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter and evolution, are used to flag a pigmented lesion as suspicious for melanoma.
needed: The ABCD rule (asymmetry, irregular borders, varied colours, diameter over 6 mm) plus E for evolution identifies features of skin lesions indicative of melanoma.

claim: How quickly the cells were dividing under the microscope matters too, because more dividing cells generally means a worse outlook.
needed: Mitotic count is an important independent prognostic factor for localised primary melanoma, with an inverse correlation between mitotic rate and survival.

claim: BRAF testing is routinely sent on every stage IA melanoma at presentation so the mutation status is known early.
needed: NICE: do not offer BRAF analysis of tissue from stage IA or IB primary melanoma at presentation except in a clinical trial; carry it out for stage IIC to IV.

claim: In advanced BRAF-mutant melanoma, combining a BRAF inhibitor with a MEK inhibitor is more active than a BRAF inhibitor alone, which is why the combination is standard.
needed: The standard of care for advanced BRAF-mutant melanoma is BRAF plus MEK inhibitor combination, shown in three phase III trials to be more active than single-agent BRAF inhibitor.

claim: Stage four means the melanoma has got into the lymph nodes near where it started.
needed: Stage III melanoma is regional lymph node metastasis; stage IV is distant metastasis.

claim: Whether it's called superficial spreading or nodular doesn't really change the outlook much once we know how thick it is.
needed: The common melanoma subtypes (superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna) have little, if any, prognostic significance independent of tumour thickness.

claim: After complete resection of stage III melanoma, adjuvant immunotherapy or targeted therapy improves relapse-free survival.
needed: In completely resected stage III or IV melanoma, adjuvant immunotherapy and targeted therapies have been shown to improve RFS (level 1, grade A).

claim: The International Prognostic Index is built from five factors: age, serum LDH, performance status, stage and extranodal involvement.
needed: The IPI consists of five clinical variables: age, serum LDH, performance status, stage and extranodal involvement.

claim: An IPI score of 3 puts DLBCL in the low-intermediate risk group.
needed: IPI risk groups: 0-1 low, 2 low-intermediate, 3 high-intermediate, 4-5 high risk.

claim: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults, and it mostly turns up in older people.
needed: DLBCL is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma among adults (the most common aggressive lymphoma), with a median age at diagnosis of about 70.

claim: This kind of lymphoma usually shows up as a painful, tender lump.
needed: The most common presentation of DLBCL is a rapidly enlarging, non-painful mass, and a non-tender mass is the common examination finding.

claim: An excision biopsy is the preferred first diagnostic procedure for suspected non-Hodgkin lymphoma, with needle core biopsy kept for when surgery's risks outweigh its benefit.
needed: NICE: consider excision biopsy as the first diagnostic procedure for suspected NHL, and needle core biopsy when the risk of surgery outweighs the benefit of excision.

claim: A quick fine-needle test is usually all we need to diagnose the exact type of lymphoma.
needed: Needle biopsies often don't remove enough tissue to diagnose lymphoma or its type, so most doctors don't use them for diagnosis; excisional biopsy is preferred.

claim: With standard immunochemotherapy, germinal centre B-cell-like DLBCL has a more favourable outcome than the activated B-cell-like subtype.
needed: Patients with GCB DLBCL have more favourable outcomes than those with ABC DLBCL when treated with standard immunochemotherapy.

claim: R-CHOP isn't really the standard anymore, because the newer intensified regimens have been shown to beat it.
needed: R-CHOP remains the standard of care for most DLBCL patients; attempts to improve on it with dose intensification and novel agents have been largely futile.

claim: This lymphoma can be cured in about two out of every three people.
needed: DLBCL is curable in about two-thirds of patients; the majority are cured with combination chemoimmunotherapy.

claim: Relapsed DLBCL that is chemosensitive should be consolidated with an autologous stem cell transplant if the patient is fit enough.
needed: NICE: offer consolidation with autologous stem cell transplantation to people with chemosensitive DLBCL (at least a partial response) who are fit enough for transplantation.

claim: Double-hit lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements does about as well with standard chemotherapy as ordinary DLBCL.
needed: Double/triple-hit high-grade B-cell lymphoma (MYC with BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangement) has a poor outcome when treated with standard chemotherapy.

claim: If clinical examination and CT suggest DLBCL is confined to stage I, a PET-CT should be done to confirm that staging.
needed: NICE: offer FDG-PET-CT to confirm staging for people diagnosed with stage I DLBCL by clinical and CT criteria.

claim: With this type of lymphoma it's almost always in the bone marrow as well.
needed: DLBCL has a low frequency of bone marrow infiltration.

claim: Spread to the brain is uncommon with this lymphoma, but when it does happen it's very serious.
needed: CNS relapse in DLBCL is uncommon (lower risk than Burkitt lymphoma) but devastating, with overall survival under 6 months.

claim: The strongest known risk factor for this kind of lymphoma is having a weakened immune system.
needed: Immunodeficiency is the most potent risk factor for developing DLBCL.

claim: A Gleason score is made by adding together the two most dominant grade patterns seen in the tumour.
needed: The Gleason score corresponds to the sum of the two dominant grades (growth patterns).

claim: Three plus four and four plus three both add up to seven, so they behave exactly the same.
needed: Gleason 4+3=7 has a significantly worse prognosis than 3+4=7, which is why they fall into different Grade Groups.

claim: Even though the Gleason scale goes up to ten, six is the lowest score that's actually given nowadays.
needed: The Gleason system ranges from 2 to 10, but 6 is the lowest score currently assigned.

claim: Active surveillance should be offered for CPG1 low-risk localised prostate cancer.
needed: NICE: for CPG1 localised prostate cancer offer active surveillance, considering radical treatment only if surveillance is unsuitable or unacceptable.

claim: Active surveillance is a reasonable option for CPG4 localised prostate cancer.
needed: NICE: do not offer active surveillance to people with CPG4 and 5 localised and locally advanced prostate cancer.

claim: Keeping an eye on it means regular PSA blood tests, examinations, an MRI and repeat biopsies, instead of treating it straight away.
needed: Active surveillance in the NHS includes multiparametric MRI, regular serum PSA testing, digital rectal examination and rebiopsy, without active treatment.

claim: For a man suspected of having localised prostate cancer, a multiparametric MRI should be the first test, ahead of any biopsy.
needed: NICE: offer multiparametric MRI as the first-line investigation for people with suspected clinically localised prostate cancer.

claim: Even if the MRI comes back completely clear, a biopsy is always still needed.
needed: With an MRI Likert score of 1 or 2 (negative mpMRI), omitting prostate biopsy can be considered after discussing risks and benefits.

claim: Black men and men whose relatives had prostate cancer are more likely to get it themselves.
needed: African American men (African family background) and men with a family history of prostate cancer have an increased risk of prostate cancer.

claim: After a radical prostatectomy, biochemical recurrence is defined as a PSA rise of 2 ng/mL above the nadir.
needed: After radical prostatectomy, recurrence is two consecutive PSA values above 0.2 ng/mL and rising; nadir plus 2 ng/mL is the Phoenix definition used after radiotherapy.

claim: A rising PSA on its own after treatment doesn't automatically mean the treatment has to change straight away.
needed: Biochemical relapse (a rising PSA) alone should not mean an immediate change in treatment is needed.

claim: The hormone injections shouldn't have any effect on your sex drive.
needed: Long-term androgen deprivation will cause a reduction in libido and possible loss of sexual function.

claim: Bisphosphonates are not routinely given to prevent osteoporosis in men on androgen deprivation therapy, but they are offered to those who already have osteoporosis.
needed: NICE: do not routinely offer bisphosphonates to prevent osteoporosis in people on ADT; offer them to people on ADT who have osteoporosis.

claim: Prostate cancer bone metastases are typically osteolytic, eating away at the bone.
needed: Prostate cancer cells prevalently cause osteoblastic lesions, characterised by an excess of bone formation.

claim: If someone newly diagnosed with prostate cancer has bone pain, a bone scan is part of the first round of tests, whatever treatment is planned.
needed: A bone scan is indicated in the initial work-up, irrespective of planned treatment, if there is bone pain, locally advanced disease, or Gleason grade 4/5 with PSA of at least 10.

claim: Papillary thyroid cancer has an excellent outlook; about 99 out of 100 people are still alive ten years on.
needed: The 10-year survival rate for papillary thyroid cancer is 99%.

claim: Follicular thyroid carcinoma can be diagnosed on FNA cytology, because capsular and vascular invasion are visible on the smear.
needed: Capsular and vascular invasion, the key diagnostic features of follicular carcinoma, are not detectable on cytology, so FNA can only report a 'follicular neoplasm'.

claim: Thyroglobulin should be measured in every patient after surgery for differentiated thyroid cancer, waiting at least six weeks after the operation.
needed: Serum Tg should be checked in all postoperative patients with DTC, but not earlier than six weeks after surgery.

claim: Everyone who has an operation for thyroid cancer needs radioactive iodine afterwards, even for tiny tumours under a centimetre.
needed: NICE: do not offer RAI for T1a or T1b tumours (including multifocal) unless there are adverse features, regional lymph node involvement or other metastatic disease.

claim: After total thyroidectomy and RAI, thyroid hormone is dosed to suppress TSH below 0.1 mIU/L until the 9 to 12 month review.
needed: NICE: offer thyroid hormone at doses suppressing TSH below 0.1 mIU/L after total or completion thyroidectomy and RAI, continued until review at 9 to 12 months.

claim: With an excellent response to treatment, TSH should stay suppressed below 0.1 mIU/L for life.
needed: With an excellent response, TSH suppression is reduced to a target of 0.3 to 2.0 mIU/L and continued for life; below 0.1 is for persistent or recurrent disease.

claim: Once the thyroid has been taken out and the radioactive iodine given, a thyroglobulin blood level that's still detectable can mean some thyroid tissue or cancer is left behind.
needed: Detectable thyroglobulin in people without thyroglobulin antibodies suggests residual thyroid tissue or residual or recurrent thyroid cancer.

claim: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is driven by BRAF mutations rather than RET.
needed: Medullary thyroid cancer, sporadic or inherited, results from mutation of the RET proto-oncogene.

claim: Total thyroidectomy is recommended for thyroid cancers over 4 cm, or of any size with multifocal or bilateral disease, extrathyroidal spread, or involved nodes or distant metastases.
needed: Total thyroidectomy is recommended for tumours over 4 cm, or any size with multifocal, bilateral, extrathyroidal (pT3/pT4a) or familial disease, or involved nodes and/or distant metastases.

claim: Even with a small, low-risk papillary cancer, we always have to go back and take out the rest of the thyroid.
needed: Completion thyroidectomy is not needed in low-risk, unifocal, intrathyroidal tumours under 4 cm with clinically negative lymph nodes.

claim: Lumps in the thyroid are really common and most of them aren't cancer; only something like 7 to 15 in every 100 turn out to be.
needed: Thyroid nodules are very common, and thyroid cancer occurs in about 7-15% of them.

claim: Anaplastic thyroid cancer usually has a good outlook, much like the papillary type.
needed: Anaplastic thyroid cancer is always considered stage IV and its prognosis is generally regarded as poor.

claim: Guiding the needle with ultrasound gives more accurate thyroid biopsy results, with fewer complications, than doing it by feel.
needed: Ultrasound-guided FNA of thyroid nodules is more accurate and less complicated than palpation-guided FNA.

claim: Things like past radiation exposure and having relatives with thyroid cancer make papillary thyroid cancer more likely.
needed: Common risk factors for papillary thyroid cancer are radiation exposure, family history of thyroid cancer and iodine deficiency.

claim: Prophylactic central level VI neck dissection isn't recommended for small low-risk papillary cancers because it raises the risk of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and permanent hypoparathyroidism.
needed: Prophylactic level VI dissection carries a higher incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve damage and permanent hypoparathyroidism and is not recommended in low-risk, small papillary cancers.

claim: Wearing an underwire bra can raise your risk of breast cancer.
needed: Evidence on whether wearing underwire bras is associated with breast cancer risk.

claim: Antiperspirant deodorants are one of the things that cause breast cancer.
needed: Evidence on whether antiperspirant or deodorant use is a cause of breast cancer.

claim: Patients can usually resume driving two weeks after a laparoscopic colectomy for colon cancer.
needed: Guidance on when patients can return to driving after laparoscopic colorectal cancer surgery.

claim: Eating a lot of spicy food is one of the causes of bowel cancer.
needed: Evidence on whether spicy food consumption is associated with colorectal cancer risk.

claim: Tattoo pigment over a naevus impairs dermoscopic assessment and can delay the diagnosis of melanoma.
needed: Evidence on whether tattoos overlying naevi interfere with dermoscopy or delay melanoma diagnosis.

claim: Regular coffee consumption is associated with a reduced risk of cutaneous melanoma.
needed: Epidemiological evidence on coffee or caffeine intake and cutaneous melanoma risk.

claim: Once you've been treated for lymphoma you can never give blood again.
needed: Blood donation eligibility rules for people previously treated for lymphoma.

claim: Commercial air travel is contraindicated while a patient is receiving R-CHOP for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
needed: Guidance on the safety of air travel during R-CHOP chemotherapy.

claim: Prostate cancer can be passed on to a partner through sex.
needed: Evidence on whether prostate cancer can be transmitted to a sexual partner.

claim: Radiofrequency exposure from mobile phones is an established cause of differentiated thyroid cancer.
needed: Evidence on whether mobile phone radiofrequency exposure causes thyroid cancer.
